source.title: LUNE: Efficient LLM Unlearning via LoRA Fine-Tuning with Negative Examples
source.authors: Yezi Liu; Hanning Chen; Wenjun Huang; Yang Ni; Mohsen Imani

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether paraphrased adversarial prompts elicit targeted content after unlearning, using its own unlearning methods and an adversarial-probe rejection measure.
record.gate_note: The directly relevant results are the reported adversarial probe rejection rates (APR), including comparisons across unlearning methods and negative-example quality. The study does not compare recovery against a model that never learned the target. Its USR, GUR, and MIA results do not directly measure recovery under the specified attacks. Quantization, activation-direction ablation, and fine-tuning attacks are not tested.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper (LUNE). Its Adversarial Probe Rejection Rate (APR) gives the share of paraphrased probes that do not regenerate target content. It reports APR for eight unlearning methods on four benchmarks, plus Yao-Neg (LoRA) in Table 8 and LUNE with weaker negatives in Table 5. 100−APR is a paraphrase-elicitation rate, and it can be set against direct-prompt leakage (100−USR) in the same tables. This bears on E (recovery by rephrasing) and on F, for LUNE's paraphrase robustness only. The test is weak: paraphrase is the only attack, there is no pre-unlearning reference, and how the probes were built is barely described.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that LUNE gives strong unlearning (USR/APR), the best utility retention (GUR) on all four datasets and the lowest MIA on most of them. They claim this comes at about an order of magnitude less compute, but argue it from parameter counts and report no measured timings. They also conclude that clear, specific negative examples matter. They do not note that APR is below USR for every method including LUNE, i.e. that paraphrasing leaks more target content than direct prompts. They test no relearning, quantization or ablation attacks.
record.recipe_differences: LUNE uses negative-example LoRA fine-tuning with a frozen backbone; the paper's APR evaluation uses paraphrased probes. It does not reproduce the named original methods' recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: On RWKU, APR changes with negative-example quality: high-quality 79.4%, medium-quality 67.2%, and low-quality 53.9%.

fits_no_version.finding: MIA accuracy after unlearning stays at 17–35% across methods (Table 3), and reaches 32.0% for LUNE with low-quality negatives (Table 5). Lower is better, but no chance reference is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Membership-inference leakage persists after unlearning (a privacy residue rather than knowledge recovery).

record.problems: APR measures rejection of target outputs, but the study gives no never-trained model comparison, so it cannot establish whether any residual elicitation exceeds that reference. The only reported attack type relevant here is paraphrasing; APR uncertainty is not stated for the example-quality comparison.
record.rows_left_out: USR, GUR, and MIA results were not extracted as rows because they do not measure recovery under the attacks in the claim. Figure 3's negative-versus-irrelevant-example APR values were not extracted because they are presented in a figure rather than as separately tabulated APR results; Table 3 and Table 5 provide the corresponding tabulated findings.

untested.parts: No targeted-knowledge accuracy relative to chance and no standard capability benchmark. USR counts prompts that no longer yield the target output, and GUR is a utility ratio against the original model. The paraphrase result is recorded under E. No relearning, quantization or ablation attacks.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.

No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of blocking versus deletion. LUNE keeps the backbone frozen and calls its updates reversible, so by construction the knowledge stays in the base weights. This is not tested.

Jailbreaks, other languages and in-context information are not tested. Only paraphrased probes are used, their generation is not described, and there is no pre-unlearning APR to show how much of the original knowledge comes back.
LUNE is not evaluated against fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization, jailbreaks, multilingual or in-context attacks.

missing.what: USR (direct-prompt unlearning success) for every method, dataset and negative-quality setting. It is the baseline for paraphrase leakage (APR). The per-row values are given in row_fixes.
missing.locator: Table 3, Table 5 and Table 8 USR rows

missing.what: Full fine-tuning variant of the negative-only objective: APR 79.5/76.0/80.2/77.3 vs USR 88.7/85.1/89.0/86.4 (EDU-RELAT/RWKU/KnowUnDo/TOFU), paraphrase gaps of 8.8–9.2 points. No uncertainty is given.

APR and USR when trained on irrelevant rather than negative examples. Likely APR 68.1/65.9/69.3/67.2 vs USR 75.4/72.0/76.8/74.5 (EDU-RELAT/RWKU/KnowUnDo/TOFU). The pairing is inferred from the extracted figure labels and is uncertain.

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) Rule 1: the list and range row_fixes items (R01-R07/R09-R15/R17-R23/R25-R31, R08/R16/R24/R32, R34/R35, R36-R39) are now one item per row. Each item gives that row's own USR baseline and its direct vs paraphrased leakage, recomputed from Tables 3, 5 and 8. States and version links are unchanged.
(2) The earlier labels said paraphrase adds 'about 3–10 points' of leakage. The text gives 4.7 points (Yao-Neg full-FT KnowUnDo) to 11.7 points (Yao-Neg full-FT EDU-RELAT).
(3) The earlier verdict gave E both 'supports' and 'limits_scope' on the same condition group, while every E row is 'partial'. I replaced the pair with one E limits_scope label over all 39 E rows. The direction is consistent (paraphrase leaks more in 39/39 comparisons) but the effect is modest: most probes are still rejected, and with no pre-unlearning reference the recovery cannot be measured against the original knowledge.
(4) The F reason now adds that LUNE's USR−APR gap (7.9–9.1 points) is within the baselines' range. Its higher APR therefore tracks its higher USR, not a paraphrase-specific robustness. This is my inference from Table 3.
(5) authors_conclusion: the order-of-magnitude compute saving rests on a complexity argument; no timings are reported.
(6) Smaller edits: Table 5 added to the USR 'missing' locator; tentative Figure 3 values added; untested C notes that the frozen backbone and 'reversible' updates mean the knowledge is suppressed by design.
Kept from the earlier verdict: relation, tranche, the MIA fits_no_version item, and its other caveats. The reader's 'challenges' reading of E misreads APR, since high rejection does not mean paraphrase recovers nothing. APR's target set T is 'known target outputs', and the matching rule is unspecified. The ± values are standard errors of the mean over three seeds (Appendix B.1). Eq. 1 minimises −log P(y−|x), which raises the likelihood of the counterfactual answers. So LUNE is relabelling-style suppression, which its own related-work section says can 'merely suppress outputs'.
No instructions addressed to the reader were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports unlearning success and utility metrics, but does not report targeted-knowledge accuracy relative to chance or test the full version's combined condition.
No post-unlearning relearning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or subset-of-forgotten-facts examples is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or test of whether unlearning blocks access rather than deletes knowledge is reported.
Only paraphrased adversarial prompts are tested; jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context information are not.
The proposed method is evaluated against paraphrased adversarial prompts only, not fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.

relationships.condition: Paraphrased probes vs direct prompts, across nine unlearning methods (GA, NPO, TV, SKU, Yao-Neg full-FT and LoRA, LoKU, MemFlex, LUNE) and LUNE with weaker negatives, on EDU-RELAT, RWKU and TOFU (Mistral-7B) and KnowUnDo (LLaMA-2 7B)
relationships.reason: Paraphrase leaks more than direct prompts in all 39 comparisons, by 4.7–11.7 points (GA RWKU 31.1%→39.0%), but 54–84% of probes are still rejected and there is no pre-unlearning reference (R01–R39; USR from Tables 3, 5 and 8).
relationships.display_finding: Leakage rose by 4.7–11.7 points in all 39 comparisons, including GA RWKU increasing from 31.1% to 39.0%, while 54–84% of probes remained rejected and restoration lacked a pre-unlearning reference.

source_check.reason: Checked: USR minus APR is 4.7 (Yao-Neg full-FT KnowUnDo) to 11.7 (Yao-Neg full-FT EDU-RELAT) in all 39 comparisons (R33 repeats R16), and APR is 53.9-84.2. Recovery is consistent but incomplete, with no pre-unlearning reference, so limits_scope is right.

relationships.condition: LUNE under paraphrased probes on four datasets, and on RWKU with high-, medium- and low-quality negatives
relationships.reason: LUNE has the top APR on 3/4 datasets, yet paraphrase elicits target content on 16–21% of probes vs 8–12% direct. Its USR−APR gap (7.9–9.1 points) sits inside the baselines' range, and APR drops to 67.2/53.9 with weaker negatives (R08, R16, R24, R32, R33, R34, R35).
relationships.display_finding: LUNE leads APR on 3/4 datasets but paraphrases elicit target content on 16–21% of probes versus 8–12% directly, its USR−APR gap of 7.9–9.1 points lies within the baseline range, and weaker negatives reduce APR to 67.2 and 53.9.
